lf-timeline.description: An authored sequence of events over time, one lane per actor, that the reader steps through with Previous and Next while a playhead and a step list follow. Use it to explain an order of events, such as a race between jobs, or to compare several runs of the same sequence on one time axis, such as before and after a fix; use `lf-trace` for a recorded browser journey and `lf-motion` for continuous playback.
lf-timeline.x-instructions: Write one `lf-lane` per actor, in the order the reader should scan them, and in each an `lf-event` per thing that happened to it. `at` is the event's time in milliseconds from the sequence's start; add `end` for an event with duration, such as work in progress, and leave it out for an instant. Previous and Next visit events in start order: events with the same `at` share one step, and a span's end is not a step, so model a moment the reader must stop at, such as a write landing, as its own instant. Name each event with a `<strong>` holding a short clause, since the prose around the widget carries the explanation; the widget lays the names out so that none overlaps a bar, another name or the playhead. Give every event a page-unique `id`: it is the event's comment target.
lf-timeline.x-example: BuildCompileArtifact readyReleaseRoll out

lf-lane.description: One actor's row in an `lf-timeline`, opening with the `<strong>` that names the actor, then holding its events.

lf-run.description: One run of a compared sequence in an `lf-timeline`, such as the run before a fix, opening with the `<strong>` that names it, then holding its lanes. Every run in a timeline shares its time axis and its playhead, and a timeline with runs keeps every lane in one.
lf-run.x-example: Before the fixClientSendResendServerApplyApply againAfter the fixClientSendResendServerApplySkip the duplicate

lf-event.description: One event in a timeline lane: an instant at `at`, or a span from `at` to `end`, in milliseconds, holding only the `<strong>` that names it.
